text: NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) is the storage interface protocol designed for flash memory, replacing the queueing architecture inherited from spinning disks. Because each NVMe queue can hold thousands of outstanding commands, a single NVMe SSD sustains more than a million IOPS at sub-millisecond latency.

An all-flash array (AFA) builds every tier out of SSDs, eliminating the rotational latency and seek time of spinning media. Modern AFAs deliver deterministic single-digit-millisecond latency at high IOPS, which is why checkpoint-heavy AI workloads usually run on flash before data ages out to cheaper media.

During distributed training, checkpoints can reach terabyte scale within minutes. Tiered checkpointing writes first to fast local or attached NVMe, then asynchronously moves the checkpoint to durable object storage, so the training loop never stalls on a slow write path.

Object storage exposes buckets and objects over a REST API and is the natural landing zone for training datasets and cold checkpoints. It scales to petabytes with erasure coding and a flat operations model, at the cost of higher read latency than block storage.

Erasure coding splits each object into k data shards and m parity shards and reconstructs the object from any k of the k+m pieces. Compared with three-way replication, erasure coding cuts capacity overhead from about 3x to roughly 1.2 to 1.3x, trading extra CPU on repair reads and recovery.

Lustre is a distributed parallel filesystem that aggregates many storage targets behind a single namespace. Because file I/O is striped across targets, HPC jobs see aggregate throughput in the gigabytes per second, which is why Lustre remains the default shared filesystem for large training datasets.

Ingestion pipelines validate, deduplicate, and shard raw data before training. Pre-sharding into fixed-size self-contained records avoids the small-file IOPS cliff, where millions of tiny files overwhelm metadata servers and throttle dataset reads.

GPU training clusters pair compute nodes with high-bandwidth fabrics such as InfiniBand or RoCE for gradient traffic. Storage traffic is usually kept on a separate network path so checkpoint writes and dataset loads do not contend with model-parallel communication.

Storage tiering moves data between hot, warm, and cold tiers based on access recency and frequency. AI platforms commonly cache the active dataset in NVMe, checkpoint to flash, and archive older checkpoints to object storage to control cost without sacrificing read speed.

IOPS counts how many requests per second a storage tier sustains, while latency measures the time from request to response. Checkpoint writes need high sustained throughput, and dataset reads during training need steady IOPS without tail-latency spikes that would leave GPUs idle.

A lakehouse layer combines object-storage economics with structured warehouse semantics such as schemas, SQL, and transactional commits. Teams use it to curate training datasets, version them, and reuse the same platform for analytics without maintaining a separate data warehouse.

Ceph is a unified distributed storage system that serves object, block, and file interfaces from one object store. Data placement and self-healing are driven by CRUSH maps, so capacity can be added by simply attaching new hosts.

Lossless compression reduces capacity and network transfer for datasets that are read repeatedly. lz4 favors very fast decompression for training-read paths, while zstd achieves a better ratio for archives and cold backups where decode speed matters less.

RAID 5 and RAID 6 stripe data across spinning disks with one or two parity blocks. They are capacity-efficient for bulk cold data, but rebuild time grows with disk size, so all-flash deployments usually rely on smaller, faster mirrors instead.

Vector databases index high-dimensional embeddings for similarity search, the retrieval step in RAG pipelines. Approximate nearest-neighbor indexes accept a small recall loss in exchange for orders-of-magnitude speedups over brute-force exact search across the full corpus.
